problems.title: Uniform perturbations control suprema
problems.objective: Prove that uniformly close bounded functions have suprema differing by at most their uniform error.
problems.statement: Let E be nonempty and let f,g:E→ℝ be bounded. If |f(x)-g(x)|≤ε for every x∈E, where ε≥0, prove |sup_E f-sup_E g|≤ε. Deduce that uniform convergence f_n→f implies sup_E f_n→sup_E f whenever all functions are bounded.
problems.strategy: Convert the pointwise uniform-error inequality into two upper-bound inequalities, one for each supremum, and then apply the estimate to f_n and f with ε=‖f_n-f‖∞.
hints: From f(x)≤g(x)+ε, what upper bound for f(E) is supplied by sup_E g+ε?
Repeat the argument after swapping f and g to obtain the reverse one-sided inequality.
For the convergence deduction, use the single index N supplied by uniform convergence and apply the supremum estimate for every n≥N.
problems.solution: For every x, f(x)≤g(x)+ε≤sup_E g+ε, so sup_E f≤sup_E g+ε. Swapping f and g gives sup_E g≤sup_E f+ε. These inequalities are equivalent to |sup_E f-sup_E g|≤ε. If f_n→f uniformly, then ε_n:=sup_{x∈E}|f_n(x)-f(x)| tends to 0, and the established estimate gives |sup_E f_n-sup_E f|≤ε_n→0.
rubricCriteria: Derives both one-sided supremum inequalities from the pointwise error bound.
Combines the inequalities to obtain the absolute-value estimate without assuming a maximizer exists.
Applies the estimate to the uniform errors and concludes convergence of the suprema.

problems.flawedProof: Choose x_f and x_g where f and g attain their suprema. Since |f(x_f)-g(x_f)|≤ε, we have sup f-sup g≤ε, and this proves the result. This fails because neither supremum is assumed to be attained and it also omits the reverse inequality.

problems.title: Moving spikes defeat termwise integration
problems.objective: Construct continuous triangular spikes that converge pointwise to zero while their suprema grow and their integrals remain one.
problems.statement: For n≥1 define f_n:[0,1]→ℝ by f_n(x)=n²x for 0≤x≤1/n, f_n(x)=n(2-nx) for 1/n<x≤2/n, and f_n(x)=0 for 2/n<x≤1. Prove each f_n is continuous, f_n(x)→0 for every x∈[0,1], convergence is not uniform, and ∫_0^1 f_n(x)dx=1 for every n≥2.
problems.strategy: Verify the pieces agree at both breakpoints, show every fixed positive x eventually lies beyond the shrinking support, and compute the area as two triangles of total base 2/n and height n.
hints: Evaluate the left and right formulas at x=1/n and x=2/n before claiming continuity.
For a fixed x>0, choose n>2/x; then x lies outside the support. Treat x=0 separately.
The maximum occurs at x=1/n. For the integral, either integrate both linear pieces or use the area of the triangular graph.
problems.solution: At x=1/n both nonzero formulas equal n, and at x=2/n the second formula equals 0, so the pieces join continuously. Also f_n(0)=0. If x>0, then n>2/x implies x>2/n and hence f_n(x)=0; thus f_n→0 pointwise. But f_n(1/n)=n, so ‖f_n‖∞=n and convergence to 0 is not uniform. For n≥2 the support is contained in [0,1], and direct integration gives ∫_0^{1/n}n²x dx=1/2 and ∫_{1/n}^{2/n}n(2-nx)dx=1/2, for total 1.
rubricCriteria: Checks continuity at both moving breakpoints and handles x=0 in the pointwise limit.
Uses a fixed-x eventual-support argument for pointwise convergence and the peak value for nonuniformity.
Computes both integral pieces correctly and notes why n≥2 keeps the full support inside [0,1].

problems.objective: Carry out the rational-point diagonal argument and use equicontinuity to obtain uniform convergence.
problems.statement: Outline why a uniformly bounded equicontinuous sequence on [0,1] has a uniformly convergent subsequence.
problems.strategy: Enumerate a countable dense subset of [0,1], for example the rationals. Organize the argument around that step, then name each earlier theorem used and verify its compactness, integrability, completeness, or regularity hypotheses.

problems.solution: Enumerate a countable dense subset of [0,1], for example the rationals. Boundedness lets us successively choose subsequences converging at the first, second, … dense point; take the diagonal subsequence. Given ε, equicontinuity supplies a common δ and compactness supplies finitely many δ-net points. Convergence at those points plus two equicontinuity errors makes the diagonal subsequence uniformly Cauchy. Completeness of C[0,1] supplies a uniform limit.

problems.title: Analytic Fourier synthesis
problems.objective: Use exponential coefficient decay and the M-test to justify every finite order of termwise differentiation.
problems.statement: If |c_n|≤Cρ^{|n|}, 0<ρ<1, prove Σc_ne^{inx} is uniformly differentiable termwise any finite number of times.
problems.strategy: The kth derivative terms are bounded by C|n|^kρ^{|n|}, a summable sequence. Organize the argument around that step, then name each earlier theorem used and verify its compactness, integrability, completeness, or regularity hypotheses.
hints: Write the definitions and domain restrictions for “Analytic Fourier synthesis” before performing the main calculation.
The useful first move is to establish this intermediate fact: the kth derivative terms are bounded by c|n|^kρ^{|n|}, a summable sequence.
Name each earlier theorem used and verify its compactness, integrability, completeness, or regularity hypotheses.
problems.solution: After k formal differentiations, the nth term is (in)^kc_ne^{inx}, whose norm is at most C|n|^kρ^{|n|}. The two-sided numerical series Σ_{n∈ℤ}|n|^kρ^{|n|} converges by the ratio test: a polynomial factor cannot defeat exponential decay. The M-test therefore gives uniform convergence of every kth derivative series. Starting with uniform convergence at k=0 and applying the termwise differentiation theorem inductively proves that the sum is C^k for every finite k and that each derivative is the corresponding termwise series.

theorem ra2_300 {c : ℤ → ℂ} {C ρ : ℝ} (hC : 0 ≤ C) (hρ0 : 0 < ρ) (hρ1 : ρ < 1)

      _ = C*|n|^k*ρ^(Int.natAbs n) := by ring
  exact Summable.of_nonneg_of_le (fun n => norm_nonneg _) hterm
    (summable_natAbs_pow_mul_geometric hC hρ0 hρ1 k)
